Where there is no sidewalk, walkers walk on the left facing traffic and step off the pavement for cars.

scenario.text: Jada needs to cross a busy street in the middle of a long block, far from the corners.

reasoning.text: Walkers never cross mid-block between intersections, and they look both ways before crossing.

result.text: Jada walks to the corner, waits on the curb for WALK, looks both ways, and crosses keeping right in the crosswalk.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a pedestrian always has the right-of-way, wherever they cross.

correction.text: A walker crossing outside an intersection crosswalk, or skipping a provided tunnel or overpass, yields to every vehicle.

rationale.text: Sidewalks come first; without them, walk on the left facing traffic and step off the pavement for approaching cars.

narration.text: This lesson opens the section on pedestrian safety with the rules for people on foot. Pedestrians, like drivers, have signals to obey and places where they may and may not cross. We will look at how walkers follow traffic and pedestrian signals and where they wait, the ban on crossing in the middle of a block, keeping right in a crosswalk, looking both ways, where to walk when there is a sidewalk and when there is not, and whom a walker must yield to when crossing outside a crosswalk or skipping a tunnel or overpass that has been provided.

lines.text: Wait on the curb, not the street.

narration.text: Walkers obey traffic signals unless pedestrian signals tell them otherwise. While waiting for a green light or a WALK signal, they wait on the curb, not in the street. Walkers never cross in the middle of a block, between intersections. Inside a crosswalk, they keep to the right where possible. Before crossing, and before stepping out from behind a parked car, they look both ways. So the steps are simple: go to the corner, wait on the curb, follow the signal, look both ways, and keep right as you cross. Those are the handbook's crossing rules for walkers at signals.

title.text: Where to walk; when to yield

narration.text: Where there is a sidewalk, walkers use it. Where there is none, they walk on the left side of the road, facing traffic, and step off the pavement when a car approaches. A walker who crosses outside an intersection crosswalk yields to every vehicle. So does a walker who skips a pedestrian tunnel or overpass that has been provided and crosses the road instead. So where a walker crosses matters: outside an intersection crosswalk, or bypassing a provided tunnel or overpass, the walker yields to every vehicle on the road.

lines.text: Look before stepping past parked cars.

narration.text: Looking is part of every crossing. Before crossing any street, walkers look both ways. Before stepping out from behind a parked car, they look both ways again. Inside a crosswalk, they keep to the right where possible. These habits sit alongside the signal rules: walkers obey traffic signals unless pedestrian signals redirect them, and they wait on the curb, not in the street, for a green light or a WALK signal. And they never cross mid-block between intersections. So a walker crosses at the corner, from the curb, on the signal, after looking both ways, and keeps right.

Here is a trap built from walker right-of-way. Learners sometimes think pedestrians always have the right-of-way. The handbook says otherwise. A walker who crosses outside an intersection crosswalk yields to every vehicle, and so does a walker who bypasses a provided tunnel or overpass. Walkers also never cross mid-block between intersections. A second trap is where to walk on a road without sidewalks: on the left, facing traffic, not on the right with traffic. When a question describes a walker, check where they are crossing or walking before deciding who yields.

Here is a quick check: you are walking along a country road with no sidewalk. Which side of the road should you walk on? Work out your answer before reading on. Walk on the left side, facing traffic, and step off the pavement when a car approaches. Sidewalks always come first when they exist. If you then need to cross the road and there is no crosswalk, remember that a walker crossing outside a crosswalk yields to every vehicle, and that you look both ways before you cross. Walk left, facing traffic, without a sidewalk.

lines.text: Wait on the curb; obey signals.
No sidewalk: walk left, facing traffic.

narration.text: Let us sum up. Walkers obey traffic signals unless pedestrian signals redirect them, and they wait on the curb for green or WALK. They never cross mid-block between intersections, keep right inside crosswalks where possible, and look both ways before crossing and before stepping out from behind parked cars. They use sidewalks where they exist; otherwise they walk on the left facing traffic and step off the pavement for approaching cars. A walker crossing outside an intersection crosswalk, or bypassing a provided tunnel or overpass, yields to every vehicle. Next, pedestrian conduct.

why_how.text: White canes are reserved for blind, partially blind, or disabled walkers on public roads.
Walkers stay visible and careful: no darting into traffic, light clothing at night, and no walking while drinking.

scenario.text: Omar plans an evening walk home along a dark street after a party.

reasoning.text: Walkers wear white or light clothes with lights or reflectors at night and avoid walking while drinking, since alcohol feeds walker crashes.

result.text: Omar wears a light jacket with a reflector, skips the drinks, and never darts into the street.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking anyone may stand in the road to ask drivers for a ride or for money.

correction.text: Nobody stands in roads seeking rides, contributions, or business, except locally authorized charitable solicitors.

prompt.text: You get off a bus on a busy street. What does the handbook say about stepping off?

rationale.text: Walkers step carefully from buses and streetcars, never dart into vehicle paths, and enter and leave cars on the curb side.

narration.text: This lesson covers how pedestrians behave on and near the road. Some rules reserve certain things for certain walkers, like the white cane. Others ban standing in the road to ask drivers for rides, money, or business, with one exception. Then there are the safety habits the handbook asks every walker to follow: never darting into traffic, dressing to be seen at night, getting on and off buses and cars carefully, avoiding walking while drinking, and following local bans on crossing outside crosswalks in business districts and on designated highways.

lines.text: White canes: blind, partially blind or disabled.
No standing in roads for rides.

narration.text: On public roads, white canes belong only to walkers who are blind, partially blind, or disabled. Nobody may stand in a road to seek a ride, a contribution, or business, except charitable solicitors that the local government has authorized. So a white cane carries a specific meaning: the person carrying it is blind, partially blind, or disabled. And the road itself is not a place to ask drivers for anything, unless the solicitor is a charitable solicitor with local authorization. White canes and road soliciting are both narrow rules.

lines.text: Never dart into a vehicle's path.
Light clothes and reflectors at night.

narration.text: Walkers never dart into the path of a vehicle. At night, they wear white or light-colored clothes and carry lights or reflectors. They step carefully when getting off buses and streetcars, and they get in and out of cars on the curb side. They avoid walking while drinking, since alcohol feeds walker crashes. And they obey local bans on crossing outside crosswalks in business districts and on designated highways. So the habits cover visibility, care around vehicles, and alcohol, and alcohol, and they apply every time a walker is on or near the road.

lines.text: White cane: blind, partially blind or disabled.
No exceptions for rides or business.

narration.text: Here is a trap built from two narrow rules. Learners sometimes think anyone may carry a white cane for visibility at night. The handbook says white canes belong solely to blind, partially blind, or disabled walkers on public roads. For visibility at night, walkers wear white or light clothes with lights or reflectors instead. A second trap is road soliciting. Standing in the road for rides, contributions, or business is banned, and the only exception is a locally authorized charitable solicitor. When a question asks who may do either, the answer is narrow.

Here is a quick check: you get off a bus on a busy street. What does the handbook say about how you step off and move on? Work out your answer before reading on. Step carefully from the bus, and never dart into the path of a vehicle. When getting in or out of a car, use the curb side. If it is night, light clothing with lights or reflectors helps drivers see you. And if a local ban applies to crossing outside crosswalks in a business district or on a designated highway, walk to a crosswalk instead. Never dart into a vehicle's path.

lines.text: White canes: blind, partially blind or disabled.
No road soliciting but authorized charity.
No darting; be seen at night.

narration.text: To wrap up, white canes belong only to blind, partially blind, or disabled walkers on public roads, and nobody stands in roads seeking rides, contributions, or business except locally authorized charitable solicitors. Walkers never dart into vehicle paths, wear white or light clothes with lights or reflectors at night, step carefully from buses and streetcars, enter and leave cars on the curb side, avoid walking while drinking since alcohol feeds walker crashes, and follow local bans on crossing outside crosswalks in business districts and on designated highways. Next, what drivers owe pedestrians.

why_how.text: Drivers always pay special attention to persons on foot.
White canes and assistance animals mark walkers who are blind, partially blind, or disabled, and drivers take every precaution for them.

scenario.text: Near a bus stop, Lin sees a walker with an assistance animal stepping toward the crosswalk.

reasoning.text: Drivers heed assistance animals and white canes, take every precaution, and stop fully whenever only stopping avoids injury or danger.

result.text: Lin slows and comes to a full stop so the walker can cross safely.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a driver only needs to slow down, never stop, for a walker with a white cane.

correction.text: Drivers stop fully whenever only stopping avoids injury or danger to a crossing walker.

memory_support.text: Cane or animal: be ready to stop.

prompt.text: You see a walker about to step off the curb ahead. What three things does the handbook tell you to do?

answer.text: Slow down, sound the horn if needed, and be ready to stop.

rationale.text: Drivers spotting crossing walkers slow, sound horns when needed, and ready full stops; cane walkers earn every precaution up to a full stop.

narration.text: This final lesson in the section turns to drivers. The handbook asks drivers to always pay special attention to people on foot. We will look at what a driver does on seeing a walker crossing or about to cross, the meaning of white canes and assistance animals, the precautions drivers take for those walkers, when a full stop is required, and the places where drivers should watch especially for blind walkers. These duties apply everywhere, and the handbook names bus stops, intersections, business districts, and schools for the blind as places to watch especially.

When a driver spots a walker crossing, or about to cross, the driver slows down, sounds the horn when needed, and gets ready to make a full stop. Drivers take every precaution against harming a walker who is crossing or trying to cross, and they stop fully whenever stopping is the only way to avoid injury or danger. So seeing a walker near the road changes how you drive right away. It means slowing, a horn warning when needed, and readiness to stop fully if the walker steps into your path. Every precaution, and a full stop when needed.

lines.text: Canes and animals mark blind walkers.

narration.text: A white cane or an assistance animal marks a walker who is blind, partially blind, or disabled. Drivers heed them and take every precaution, stopping fully whenever only stopping avoids injury or danger. Drivers watch for blind people especially at bus stops, at intersections, in business districts, and near schools for the blind. And at all times, drivers pay special attention to persons on foot. So when you see a cane or an assistance animal, treat it as a signal to slow down and be ready to stop, and give that walker the room and time they need.

lines.text: Full stop when only stopping works.

narration.text: Here is a trap built from two levels of care. For any walker crossing or about to cross, the driver slows, sounds the horn when needed, and gets ready to stop. For a walker with a white cane or an assistance animal, the driver takes every precaution, up to a mandatory full stop whenever only stopping avoids injury or danger. Learners sometimes think slowing down is always enough. It is not. When a question asks what a driver must do, look for whether stopping is the only way to avoid harm. If it is, the answer is a full stop.

lines.text: A walker steps toward the curb.
What three things do you do?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you see a walker about to step off the curb ahead of you. What three things does the handbook tell you to do? Work out your answer before reading on. Slow down, sound the horn if it is needed, and be ready to stop fully. If the walker carries a white cane or has an assistance animal, take every precaution and stop fully whenever stopping is the only way to avoid injury or danger. Near bus stops, intersections, business districts, and schools for the blind, watch especially for blind walkers. Always pay special attention to people on foot.

lines.text: Slow, horn if needed, ready to stop.

narration.text: Let us sum up. When drivers spot walkers crossing or about to cross, they slow down, sound the horn when needed, and get ready to stop fully. White canes and assistance animals mark walkers who are blind, partially blind, or disabled, and drivers take every precaution against harming them, stopping fully whenever only stopping avoids injury or danger. Drivers watch for blind people at bus stops, intersections, business districts, and schools for the blind, and they always pay special attention to persons on foot. That completes the section on pedestrian safety.
